institutions.name: University of Paris
institutions.summary: The guild of masters and scholars that grew from the Paris schools became the model northern university and Latin Christendom's leading school of arts and theology. It was abolished in 1793, its faculties were revived within Napoleon's Université impériale in 1808, and the university was re-created in 1896.
institutions.notes: Its founding date is conventional. Masters' corporate organisation is visible c. 1150–1200, before the royal privilege of 1200 and the statutes of 1215. Abelard and Peter Lombard taught in the pre-university Paris schools (Notre-Dame, Sainte-Geneviève, Saint-Victor); those cathedral and monastic schools are Region 7 records.

institutions.name: Montpellier School of Medicine (before 1289)
institutions.summary: A medical studium, open to Arabic and Jewish learning, that grew up under the Guilhem lords of Montpellier. With Salerno it was the leading medical school of the 12th–13th centuries, and it was incorporated into the papal university in 1289.
institutions.notes: The edict of Guilhem VIII granting freedom to teach medicine is dated January 1181 (1180 old style). Medical teaching certainly predates it.

institutions.name: University of Montpellier
institutions.summary: Nicholas IV's bull Quia sapientia (26 October 1289) united Montpellier's schools of medicine, law and arts as a studium generale. The faculty of medicine stayed one of Europe's most famous, and it survived the Revolution as an École de santé.
institutions.notes: The medicine faculty went on in 1794 as an École de santé. The other faculties were abolished in 1793.

institutions.name: University of Toulouse
institutions.summary: Founded under the Treaty of Paris (Meaux) that ended the Albigensian Crusade, to combat heresy in Languedoc, with Count Raymond VII obliged to pay the masters. It later became a major school of Roman law.
institutions.notes: The founding is mixed: a treaty condition imposed by the papal legate and paid for by the count. It is recorded here as papal.

institutions.name: University of Orléans
institutions.summary: France's leading medieval school of civil law. It flourished because Honorius III's bull Super speculam (1219) barred Roman law at Paris, and it was confirmed as a studium generale in 1306.
institutions.notes: Law teaching existed before 1229. The start date follows the conventional link with the Paris dispersal of 1229–31.

institutions.name: University of Angers
institutions.summary: A law studium that grew from the Paris dispersal of 1229 and the cathedral school. It became a full four-faculty university in 1364.
institutions.notes: Its origins are disputed. It was a studium generale in practice before the 1364 bull.

institutions.name: University of Avignon
institutions.summary: Founded by Boniface VIII's bull of 1 July 1303 together with Count Charles II of Provence. It flourished as a law school in the papal city.
institutions.notes: Avignon was annexed to France in 1791. The university closed during the revolutionary abolitions of 1792–93.

institutions.name: University of Cahors
institutions.summary: Founded by John XXII, a native of Cahors. A small law-centred university until it merged into Toulouse in 1751.

institutions.name: University of Grenoble
institutions.summary: Founded by Dauphin Humbert II with a bull of Benedict XII. It faded, was revived in 1542, and was united with Valence in 1565. Napoleonic faculties revived it, and it was reconstituted in 1896.
institutions.notes: It lapsed in the late Middle Ages. It is kept as one institution here because of the shared identity across its revivals.

institutions.name: University of Orange
institutions.summary: Founded by Emperor Charles IV in the principality of Orange. It was a minor law university, and from 1573 had a Reformed academy attached under the Nassau princes.
institutions.notes: The closure date is approximate, during the revolutionary abolition.

institutions.name: University of Aix
institutions.summary: Founded by Alexander V's bull at the request of Louis II of Anjou, Count of Provence. Napoleonic faculties at Aix and Marseille were united as the University of Aix-Marseille in 1896.
institutions.notes: The faculty of sciences was at Marseille from 1854.

institutions.name: University of Dole / Besançon
institutions.summary: Founded at Dole by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, with papal confirmation by Martin V. It was the university of Franche-Comté, and Louis XIV moved it to Besançon after the French conquest.
institutions.notes: Founding is dated 1422/23 depending on the ducal letters and the bull. Teaching was disrupted when Louis XI sacked Dole in 1479.

institutions.name: University of Poitiers
institutions.summary: Founded by Eugene IV's bull at Charles VII's request while Paris was under English control. It was a major law university.

institutions.name: University of Caen
institutions.summary: Founded by John, Duke of Bedford, in the name of Henry VI of England during the English occupation of Normandy. Charles VII re-confirmed it after the French reconquest.

institutions.name: University of Bordeaux
institutions.summary: Founded by Eugene IV's bull at the request of Archbishop Pey Berland, while Gascony was still English.

institutions.name: University of Valence
institutions.summary: Founded by the Dauphin Louis (later Louis XI). Under Cujas in the 16th century it was a centre of humanist law.
institutions.notes: The papal confirmation by Pius II dates from 1459.

institutions.name: University of Nantes
institutions.summary: Founded by Pius II's bull at the request of Duke Francis II of Brittany. Its law faculty moved to Rennes in 1735.
institutions.notes: The modern University of Nantes (1962) is outside the period.

institutions.name: University of Bourges
institutions.summary: Founded by Paul II's bull at the request of Louis XI's brother Charles, Duke of Berry. In the 16th century, under Alciato, Cujas and Doneau, it was the centre of the mos gallicus, the humanist school of law.

institutions.name: University of Reims
institutions.summary: Founded by Paul III's bull at the request of Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine, archbishop of Reims. It was a Counter-Reformation university.

institutions.name: University of Douai
institutions.summary: Founded by Philip II with Paul IV's bull as a Catholic bulwark in the Spanish Netherlands, and home of the English College of William Allen. It was French from 1667. Its Napoleonic-era successor faculties moved to Lille and became the University of Lille in 1896.
institutions.notes: Continuity runs through the académie de Douai, whose faculties moved to Lille in 1887. The Lille faculty of sciences (1854) is counted here.

institutions.name: University of Pont-à-Mousson / Nancy
institutions.summary: Founded by Duke Charles III of Lorraine and Cardinal Charles of Lorraine, with Gregory XIII's bull, and entrusted to the Jesuits as the Counter-Reformation university of Lorraine. It was moved to Nancy in 1768 and revived by Napoleonic-system faculties.
institutions.notes: It had full university privileges and so is counted as a university, not a Jesuit college. Teaching opened in 1574.

institutions.name: University of Pau
institutions.summary: A royal university created in the old capital of Béarn, mainly a faculty of law. It succeeded in spirit the Protestant academy of Orthez/Lescar suppressed in 1620.
institutions.notes: The exact date of the letters patent is c. 1722–24.

institutions.name: University of Dijon
institutions.summary: Louis XV created a faculty of law at Dijon, seat of the Parlement of Burgundy, against opposition from Besançon. Napoleonic faculties revived it, and it was reconstituted in 1896.

institutions.name: University of Rennes
institutions.summary: Began when the law faculty of the University of Nantes was transferred to Rennes, seat of the Parlement of Brittany. It became the University of Rennes in 1896.

institutions.name: University of Lyon
institutions.summary: Napoleonic faculties of theology, letters and sciences were founded in Lyon within the Université impériale, joined by law (1875) and medicine (1877). They were constituted as a university in 1896.
institutions.notes: Lyon had no ancien-régime university.

institutions.name: University of Clermont
institutions.summary: Faculties of sciences and letters were established at Clermont-Ferrand in 1854 and formed the university in 1896.
institutions.notes: An earlier faculty of letters existed briefly under Napoleon.

institutions.name: Catholic University of Paris (Institut catholique)
institutions.summary: A free Catholic university opened by bishops under the law of 12 July 1875 on freedom of higher education. Founded under Mgr d'Hulst by the bishops of the Paris region.
institutions.notes: From 1880 it could not legally call itself a university and used the name 'institut' or 'facultés libres'.

institutions.name: Catholic University of Lille
institutions.summary: A free Catholic university opened by bishops under the law of 12 July 1875 on freedom of higher education. Founded with strong support from northern Catholic industrialists.
institutions.notes: From 1880 it could not legally call itself a university and used the name 'institut' or 'facultés libres'.

institutions.name: Catholic University of Lyon
institutions.summary: A free Catholic university opened by bishops under the law of 12 July 1875 on freedom of higher education. Founded by the bishops of south-eastern France.
institutions.notes: From 1880 it could not legally call itself a university and used the name 'institut' or 'facultés libres'.

institutions.name: Catholic University of the West (Angers)
institutions.summary: A free Catholic university opened by bishops under the law of 12 July 1875 on freedom of higher education. Founded by Bishop Charles-Émile Freppel.
institutions.notes: From 1880 it could not legally call itself a university and used the name 'institut' or 'facultés libres'.

institutions.name: Catholic University of Toulouse
institutions.summary: A free Catholic university opened by bishops under the law of 12 July 1875 on freedom of higher education. Founded by the bishops of south-western France.
institutions.notes: From 1880 it could not legally call itself a university and used the name 'institut' or 'facultés libres'.

institutions.name: Collège de Clermont / Louis-le-Grand
institutions.summary: The Jesuit college in Paris, endowed by Bishop Guillaume du Prat of Clermont. It taught philosophy and theology at university level in fierce rivalry with the University of Paris.
institutions.notes: After the 1762 expulsion it continued as a non-Jesuit collège of the university, Louis-le-Grand.

institutions.name: Collège Henri-IV de La Flèche
institutions.summary: The royal Jesuit college founded by Henri IV in his family château. It was one of the most prestigious colleges in France, with a full philosophy course.
institutions.notes: After 1764 it became a military school (now the Prytanée national militaire).

institutions.name: Academy of Nîmes
institutions.summary: The consistory added theology to the town's college of arts (1539), creating one of the earliest Reformed academies in France. In 1617 the national synod merged the Montpellier theology school into it.

institutions.name: Academy of Orthez (Royal University of Béarn)
institutions.summary: Founded by Queen Jeanne d'Albret of Navarre to train Reformed ministers for Béarn. It took the title Royal University of Béarn in 1583.
institutions.notes: For a time it was seated at Lescar. The dates of that move are not well established, so only Orthez is recorded.

institutions.name: Academy of Montauban / Puylaurens
institutions.summary: A Reformed academy set up by the national synods on the basis of a college opened in 1579. It was a leading Huguenot theological school.
institutions.notes: Founding is dated 1598–1600.

institutions.name: Academy of Saumur
institutions.summary: Founded by Philippe Duplessis-Mornay, governor of Saumur. It was the most famous Huguenot academy, home of Amyraldian theology and of Cappel's biblical criticism.

institutions.name: Academy of Sedan
institutions.summary: A Reformed academy in the sovereign principality of Sedan, developed from the college of 1579 under the dukes of Bouillon. It was a refuge for leading Protestant scholars.
institutions.notes: The national synod approved the academy in 1601.

institutions.name: Academy of Die
institutions.summary: A Reformed academy in Dauphiné that grew from a college of 1596.

institutions.name: Collège de France
institutions.summary: Francis I appointed royal readers in Hebrew, Greek and mathematics, independent of the Sorbonne, at Guillaume Budé's urging. It gives free public lectures without degrees.
institutions.notes: Typed as professional: it was a higher teaching body outside the university that granted no degrees. It fits none of the other categories.

institutions.name: Jardin du roi / Muséum national d'histoire naturelle
institutions.summary: Founded by Louis XIII's edict as a medicinal garden with public courses in botany, chemistry and anatomy outside the faculty of medicine. In 1793 it became the Muséum, Europe's leading centre of natural history.
institutions.notes: The garden opened to the public in 1640.

institutions.name: École des ponts et chaussées
institutions.summary: Trudaine created a drafting office under Jean-Rodolphe Perronet to train engineers of the royal Corps des ponts et chaussées. It is the world's oldest civil-engineering school.

institutions.name: École royale du génie de Mézières
institutions.summary: The military engineering school for the Corps du génie. Its mathematical training under Bossut and Monge made it the prototype of the École polytechnique.

institutions.name: École vétérinaire de Lyon
institutions.summary: The world's first veterinary school, founded by Claude Bourgelat with royal support.

institutions.name: École vétérinaire d'Alfort
institutions.summary: The second French veterinary school, founded by Bourgelat near Paris.

institutions.name: École des mines de Paris
institutions.summary: Founded to train mining engineers for the royal Corps des mines. After the Revolution it became an elite school of application for polytechniciens.
institutions.notes: The 1802 transfer to a practical school at Pesey (Savoie) and the return to Paris in 1816 are approximate.

institutions.name: École polytechnique
institutions.summary: Founded by the Convention, with Monge and Carnot, to train engineers for all state services in mathematics and science. Its professors and graduates dominated 19th-century French science.

institutions.name: École normale supérieure
institutions.summary: Created by the Convention (Lakanal's decree of 30 October 1794) to train teachers. Its short first session of 1795 had Lagrange, Laplace and Monge as teachers. Re-founded under Napoleon, it became the elite school of French letters and science.

institutions.name: Conservatoire national des arts et métiers
institutions.summary: Founded on Abbé Grégoire's proposal as a repository of machines and models. It became a centre of public higher technical teaching.

institutions.name: École des chartes
institutions.summary: A specialist school for archivists and palaeographers, founded by royal ordinance.

institutions.name: École centrale des arts et manufactures
institutions.summary: A private school founded by Alphonse Lavallée, Jean-Baptiste Dumas, Théodore Olivier and Eugène Péclet to train civil and industrial engineers for the private sector.

institutions.name: École libre des sciences politiques
institutions.summary: Founded by Émile Boutmy after the defeat of 1870 to train a new administrative and political elite.

institutions.name: École de physique et chimie industrielles
institutions.summary: A school of industrial physics and chemistry founded by the City of Paris. Pierre and Marie Curie discovered polonium and radium in its laboratories.

institutions.name: University of Leuven
institutions.summary: Founded by Martin V's bull (9 December 1425) at the request of Duke John IV of Brabant and the city. It became the great Catholic university of the Low Countries, a centre of humanism (Collegium Trilingue) and of Counter-Reformation theology. It was abolished by the French in 1797, revived as a Dutch state university in 1817, and re-founded as a Catholic university in 1834–35.
institutions.notes: Continuity is disputed. The State University (1817–35) and the Catholic University (1834) are distinct foundations, kept as one identity per the dataset rule for suppressed-and-refounded institutions.

institutions.name: Leiden University
institutions.summary: Founded by William of Orange as a reward for Leiden's resistance to the Spanish siege. It was the leading Protestant university of the 17th–18th centuries in philology, medicine (Boerhaave) and science.
institutions.notes: Formally founded in the name of Philip II by William of Orange and the States of Holland.

institutions.name: University of Franeker
institutions.summary: The second university of the Dutch Republic, founded by the States of Friesland. It was strongly Calvinist and drew many German and Hungarian students.
institutions.notes: Founding mode 'state' reflects the provincial States of Friesland.

institutions.name: University of Groningen
institutions.summary: Founded by the States of Stad en Lande with Ubbo Emmius as first rector. The first Dutch woman student, Aletta Jacobs, enrolled here.
institutions.notes: The States of the province are recorded as 'state'.

institutions.name: Utrecht University
institutions.summary: The city council raised its Illustrious School (1634) to a university. Under Voetius it was a stronghold of Reformed orthodoxy against Cartesianism.

institutions.name: University of Harderwijk
institutions.summary: The university of the Duchy of Gelderland. It was known for quick, cheap doctorates taken by foreigners, Linnaeus among them.
institutions.notes: The provincial States are recorded as 'state'.

institutions.name: Athenaeum Illustre of Amsterdam / University of Amsterdam
institutions.summary: A municipal illustrious school opened with orations by Vossius and Barlaeus. It became the municipal University of Amsterdam in 1877.
institutions.notes: Typed as academy for its long pre-university history. It has been a university since 1877.

institutions.name: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
institutions.summary: Founded by Abraham Kuyper as a Reformed (Calvinist) university free of state and church control.

institutions.name: Delft Polytechnic
institutions.summary: Founded by William II as the Royal Academy for civil engineers and colonial officials. It became the Polytechnic School in 1864.
institutions.notes: Technical University status came in 1905.

institutions.name: Ghent University
institutions.summary: Founded by William I of the United Netherlands as a state university, taught in Latin, then French.

institutions.name: University of Liège
institutions.summary: Founded by William I as a state university for the Walloon provinces.

institutions.name: Free University of Brussels
institutions.summary: Founded by Théodore Verhaegen and liberal Freemasons on the principle of free inquiry, as a counterweight to the Catholic University.

institutions.name: Université nouvelle de Bruxelles
institutions.summary: A radical free university formed by secession from the ULB. It survived until 1919.
institutions.notes: Closed 1919, outside the period.

institutions.name: University of Basel
institutions.summary: Founded with Pius II's bull (1459) at the city's request and opened on 4 April 1460, the oldest university in Switzerland. Centre of humanism and printing, later home of the Bernoulli mathematical dynasty.

institutions.name: Academy of Geneva / University of Geneva
institutions.summary: Founded by Calvin with the city council, with Beza as first rector, to train ministers for international Calvinism. It became the University of Geneva in 1873.
institutions.notes: Typed as academy. It has been a university since 1873.

institutions.name: Academy of Lausanne / University of Lausanne
institutions.summary: Founded by Bern after the conquest of Vaud to train Reformed pastors. It was the first French-speaking Protestant academy, and became a university in 1890.
institutions.notes: Founded by the city-republic of Bern (recorded as 'municipal').

institutions.name: Carolinum (Zurich)
institutions.summary: Zwingli's Prophezei, a theological school for exegesis of scripture. It developed into the Carolinum, Zurich's higher school.

institutions.name: University of Zurich
institutions.summary: Founded by the liberal canton of Zurich, the first European university founded by a democratic state. It was a pioneer in admitting women.

institutions.name: Hohe Schule / Academy of Bern
institutions.summary: The Reformed higher school founded after the Bern Disputation. It became an Academy in 1805.

institutions.name: University of Bern
institutions.summary: Founded by the liberal canton of Bern on the basis of the Academy.

institutions.name: Federal Polytechnic School (ETH Zurich)
institutions.summary: The federal polytechnic of the new Swiss state, set up by the federal law of 1854. It was a leading centre of engineering, physics and mathematics.

institutions.name: University of Fribourg
institutions.summary: A Catholic, bilingual university founded by the canton under Georges Python.

institutions.name: Academy of Neuchâtel
institutions.summary: Founded under the Prussian king, then sovereign prince of Neuchâtel. It was revived by the republican canton in 1866 and became a university in 1909.

events.title: Masters' guild emerges
events.desc: Teaching masters in the Paris schools on the Île de la Cité and the Left Bank begin to act as a corporation (approximate date).

events.title: Privilege of Philip Augustus
events.desc: After a town-gown riot, Philip II exempted scholars from royal and municipal jurisdiction and placed them under ecclesiastical courts.

events.title: Statutes of Robert of Courçon
events.desc: The papal legate Robert of Courçon issued the first statutes regulating the arts and theology curricula. They banned lecturing on Aristotle's natural philosophy.

events.title: Parens scientiarum
events.desc: Gregory IX's bull ended the strike and dispersal of 1229–31, which had sent masters to Angers, Orléans, Toulouse and Oxford. It recognised the university's right to suspend lectures and to make statutes, and it is called the university's Magna Carta.

events.title: Foundation of the Sorbonne college
events.desc: Robert de Sorbon, chaplain to Louis IX, founded a college for poor secular masters of theology. It later gave its name to the faculty of theology and to the whole university.

events.title: Condemnation of 219 propositions
events.desc: Bishop Étienne Tempier condemned 219 philosophical and theological theses taught in the arts faculty, aimed at radical Aristotelians such as Siger of Brabant.

events.title: Reform of Cardinal d'Estouteville
events.desc: The papal legate Guillaume d'Estouteville issued new statutes for all four faculties, acting with Charles VII's support.

events.title: Determinatio against Luther
events.desc: The theology faculty formally condemned Luther's teachings and became a bastion of Catholic orthodoxy and of the censorship of books.

events.title: Statutes of Henri IV
events.desc: New royal statutes reorganised the university under crown control after the Wars of Religion.

events.title: Gallican Four Articles imposed
events.desc: Louis XIV required the theology faculty to teach the Declaration of the Clergy of France limiting papal authority, and Gallicanism became official doctrine.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention
events.desc: The National Convention's decree of 15 September 1793 abolished the faculties and collèges of the Republic, ending the ancien-régime university.

events.title: Faculties within the Université impériale
events.desc: Under the law of 10 May 1806 and the decree of 17 March 1808, faculties of theology, law, medicine, sciences and letters were set up in the Académie de Paris as part of Napoleon's state monopoly on teaching. The Sorbonne housed letters, sciences and theology.

events.title: Women admitted to the Faculty of Medicine
events.desc: Madeleine Brès was authorised to enrol in medicine, alongside foreign women such as Mary Putnam and Elizabeth Garrett Anderson. Women had access to French degrees from this point.

events.title: Faculties regain corporate personality
events.desc: Decrees of 1885 gave the faculties civil personality and created a general council of faculties, a step toward re-forming universities.

events.title: University re-created (law of 10 July 1896)
events.desc: The law of 10 July 1896 grouped the state faculties of each académie into a university again. The University of Paris was formally reconstituted.

events.title: Edict of Guilhem VIII
events.desc: Guilhem VIII's edict allowed any qualified physician to teach medicine in Montpellier.

events.title: Statutes of Cardinal Conrad
events.desc: The papal legate Conrad of Urach gave the medical universitas its first statutes and placed licensing under the bishop of Maguelone.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Bull Quia sapientia of Nicholas IV erected the studium generale.

events.title: Medical school incorporated
events.desc: The existing medical universitas became the faculty of medicine of the new university.

events.title: Jardin des plantes
events.desc: Henri IV founded France's first botanical garden for teaching medicine, under Pierre Richer de Belleval.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention
events.desc: The National Convention's decree of 15 September 1793 abolished the faculties and collèges of the Republic, ending the ancien-régime university. Medical teaching resumed in 1794 as the École de santé.

events.title: Napoleonic faculties
events.desc: Faculties of medicine, sciences and letters were organised within the Université impériale. A law faculty followed in 1880.

events.title: University re-created (law of 10 July 1896)
events.desc: The law of 10 July 1896 grouped the state faculties of each académie into a university again.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Treaty of Paris (April 1229) required Raymond VII to fund 14 masters in Toulouse.

events.title: Paris masters arrive
events.desc: Masters who left Paris during the 1229 strike, including John of Garland, came to teach in the new studium.

events.title: Ius ubique docendi
events.desc: Gregory IX confirmed the studium and granted its graduates the right to teach everywhere.

events.title: Absorbs the University of Cahors
events.desc: Royal letters united the declining University of Cahors with Toulouse.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention
events.desc: The National Convention's decree of 15 September 1793 abolished the faculties and collèges of the Republic, ending the ancien-régime university.

events.title: Napoleonic faculties
events.desc: Faculties of law, sciences, letters and theology were set up in the Académie de Toulouse.

events.title: University re-created (law of 10 July 1896)
events.desc: The law of 10 July 1896 grouped the state faculties of each académie into a university again.

events.title: Law studium emerges
events.desc: Law schools in Orléans grew, swelled by masters leaving Paris.

events.title: Paris dispersal
events.desc: Masters and students leaving Paris during the 1229–31 strike settled in Orléans.

events.title: Bulls of Clement V
events.desc: Clement V, an Orléans law graduate, granted the privileges of a studium generale on the model of Toulouse.

events.title: Confirmation by Philip IV
events.desc: After resisting the papal bulls, Philip IV confirmed the university by royal letters.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention
events.desc: The National Convention's decree of 15 September 1793 abolished the faculties and collèges of the Republic, ending the ancien-régime university.

events.title: Law studium emerges
events.desc: Masters dispersing from Paris reinforced the law schools of Angers.

events.title: Paris dispersal
events.desc: Masters and students leaving Paris during the 1229–31 strike settled in Angers.

events.title: Full university status
events.desc: Urban V's bull, backed by Charles V and Louis I of Anjou, added theology and medicine and confirmed Angers as a studium generale.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention
events.desc: The National Convention's decree of 15 September 1793 abolished the faculties and collèges of the Republic, ending the ancien-régime university.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Bull of Boniface VIII established a studium generale.

events.title: Faculty of theology
events.desc: Antipope John XXIII added a faculty of theology.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention
events.desc: The National Convention's decree of 15 September 1793 abolished the faculties and collèges of the Republic, ending the ancien-régime university.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Bull of John XXII (1332) founded the studium generale.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Humbert II founded the studium with Benedict XII's bull.

events.title: Revived by Francis I's governor
events.desc: Teaching of law restarted after a long lapse.

events.title: United to Valence
events.desc: Charles IX united the university with that of Valence, and teaching at Grenoble ended.

events.title: Napoleonic faculties
events.desc: A law school opened in 1806, followed by faculties of letters and sciences in 1808 within the Université impériale.

events.title: University re-created (law of 10 July 1896)
events.desc: The law of 10 July 1896 grouped the state faculties of each académie into a university again.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Charter of Emperor Charles IV founded the studium.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Bull of Alexander V founded the studium generale.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention
events.desc: The National Convention's decree of 15 September 1793 abolished the faculties and collèges of the Republic, ending the ancien-régime university.

events.title: Napoleonic faculties
events.desc: Faculties of law and theology were restored at Aix (letters 1846, sciences at Marseille 1854).

events.title: University re-created (law of 10 July 1896)
events.desc: The law of 10 July 1896 grouped the state faculties of each académie into a university again. It became the University of Aix-Marseille.

events.title: Foundation
events.desc: Philip the Good founded the university at Dole, confirmed by Martin V.

events.title: Sack of Dole
events.desc: Louis XI's troops sacked Dole, disrupting the university until Habsburg rule restored it.

events.title: Transferred to Besançon
events.desc: Louis XIV moved the university to Besançon, the new capital of the conquered province.

events.title: Abolished by the Convention
